overview: Oviraptor philoceratops carries one of the most unfortunate names in palaeontology — "egg thief that loves ceratopsian eggs" — based on a misidentification. The original specimen was found next to a nest of eggs in Mongolia in 1923, assumed to be stealing from a Protoceratops nest. Decades later, embryos inside identical eggs were identified as Oviraptor itself — the animal was brooding its own clutch, not stealing Protoceratops eggs.

This correction transformed understanding of oviraptorosaur behaviour: Oviraptor and its relatives were not nest raiders but careful parents, brooding their eggs in a posture identical to modern birds. Oviraptor is a crested oviraptorosaur from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia (~75 Ma), about 1.5–2 metres long with a prominent cranial crest of unknown function.

fossilSites.name: Djadokhta Formation — Shabarakh Usu / Bayanzag
fossilSites.note: Campanian aeolian dune deposits with the type Oviraptor specimen on a nest and multiple additional oviraptorosaur nest sites.

articles.title: The egg thief that wasn't
articles.body: Roy Chapman Andrews' 1923 American Museum Central Asiatic Expedition found the Oviraptor skeleton on top of a Protoceratops-like nest; Andrews assumed nest raiding. The misinterpretation persisted for 70 years until Mark Norell and colleagues described embryos inside the same type of eggs in 1994 — and those embryos were oviraptorosaurs, not Protoceratops. Oviraptor was a brooding parent, not a thief.

articles.title: Cranial crest
articles.body: Oviraptor bore a prominent crest on the skull formed by the nasal and frontal bones. The crest varies in development between specimens, which may reflect age, sex or individual variation. Cassowary-like keratinous sheaths probably enlarged the bony core in life. The function is unknown; display and species recognition are the most commonly cited hypotheses.

articles.title: Parental care
articles.body: Multiple specimens of oviraptorosaurs (Citipati, Nemegtomaia and others closely related to Oviraptor) have been found in brooding posture — forelimbs spread over the egg ring, hindlimbs tucked under the body, head raised. The egg arrangement (pairs in a ring) is consistent with two functional oviducts, suggesting each female could lay two eggs at a time. This is among the strongest evidence for active parental care in non-avian dinosaurs.

fossilRecord.material: Partial skeleton and skull material historically associated with eggs.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous arid to semi-arid Gobi Desert dune and interdune deposits.
fossilRecord.evidence: Later discoveries showed oviraptorosaurs brooded eggs, changing the old “egg thief” interpretation.

record.description: Oviraptor philoceratops was an oviraptorid from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, known from one incomplete skeleton with a crushed skull found beside a nest. Many complete museum reconstructions actually represent Citipati.
facts: The eggs near the type are oviraptorosaur eggs, overturning the original idea that it was stealing Protoceratops eggs.
The holotype is less complete and has a lower crest than the animal often illustrated as Oviraptor.
Brooding is strongly evidenced across oviraptorids, but exact diet remains unresolved.

presentation.heroLead: The misnamed "egg thief" of the Gobi, known from a single crushed skeleton found lying on a nest that turned out to be its own kind's.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Oviraptor philoceratops
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of the feathered oviraptorid Oviraptor philoceratops in side view
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by PaleoNeolitic. Feathering follows evidence from related oviraptorosaurs; the crest outline, colour and much of the body proportion are interpretive because the only known skull is crushed.

animalParagraphs: Oviraptor was a lightly built, bird-like theropod with a short, deep, toothless skull, long grasping hands and a crest of some kind above the snout. It lived in the dune fields of the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia during the Campanian, alongside Protoceratops and Velociraptor. Estimates of around one and a half to two metres in length come from the single incomplete skeleton.

Its name, "egg thief", records a mistake. Roy Chapman Andrews's expedition found the skeleton in 1923 lying over a clutch of eggs assumed to belong to Protoceratops, and Osborn suggested it had been caught raiding the nest. Embryos found inside identical eggs in the 1990s showed that the eggs were oviraptorid, so the animal was almost certainly a parent, not a thief.

Oviraptor is much less well known than its fame suggests. The familiar tall-crested skeletons in museums and books are mostly the relative Citipati, described in 2001. The Oviraptor holotype has a badly crushed skull, so the exact shape of its crest and the finer details of its anatomy remain uncertain.
animalHighlights: A short, deep, toothless skull with a beak and a crest whose true outline is obscured by crushing.
Long arms and three-fingered hands with strongly curved claws, suited to grasping.
Found on a nest of oviraptorid eggs, making it a probable brooding parent rather than an egg raider.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: A toothless beak and deep jaws are compatible with plants, eggs, shellfish or small animals; no direct dietary evidence exists for Oviraptor itself.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Hindlimb and pelvic bones in the holotype and complete skeletons of related oviraptorids show a two-legged runner.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is extrapolated from partial remains; mass estimates of a few tens of kilograms are rough.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The crushed skull leaves the crest profile open; feathering is known in other oviraptorosaurs but not preserved in this specimen.

locality.name: Bayn Dzak (Flaming Cliffs)
locality.note: Djadokhta Formation. The holotype was collected by George Olsen in 1923 during the Central Asiatic Expeditions; the map shows the Flaming Cliffs area as a regional reference.

presentation.classificationSummary: Oviraptor is the name-bearing genus of Oviraptoridae and Oviraptorosauria, a group of feathered, beaked maniraptoran theropods. Its exact position within Oviraptoridae is hard to fix because the holotype is crushed; several specimens once called Oviraptor have been moved to Citipati and other genera.

related.reason: The tall-crested oviraptorid that most museum "Oviraptor" skeletons and brooding specimens actually represent.
A smaller crestless oviraptorid from the same formation known from complete skeletons.
The animal whose eggs Oviraptor was wrongly accused of stealing.

questions.title: What did the crest look like?
questions.copy: The skull is shattered and flattened. Restorations range from a low ridge to a tall Citipati-like casque, and none can be confirmed from the holotype.

questions.title: What did it eat?
questions.copy: Lizard bones were reported in the holotype's body cavity, and shellfish, eggs and plants have all been proposed. No study has settled the question.

questions.title: How much of what we know is really Oviraptor?
questions.copy: Only the holotype is securely assigned. Referred material from Zamyn Khondt and elsewhere belongs to Citipati or remains unnamed, so most published "Oviraptor" anatomy needs a second look.

review.ageReviewNote: The Djadokhta type horizon is Campanian, approximately 75-71 Ma.

residualUncertainty: The crushed type skull leaves crest reconstruction uncertain.
Much familiar anatomy belongs to Citipati.

evidence.material: Single incomplete skeleton with crushed skull associated with an egg nest.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not use Citipati specimens as Oviraptor anatomy or call it a proven egg thief.
evidence.summary: Oviraptor philoceratops was an oviraptorid from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, known from one incomplete skeleton with a crushed skull found beside a nest. Many complete museum reconstructions actually represent Citipati.
evidence.sourceBasis: Osborn (1924), original description of Oviraptor; Norell et al. (1994), dinosaur embryos and identity of oviraptorosaur eggs

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.note: An incomplete skeleton with a crushed skull, collected at Bayn Dzak in 1923 and described by Osborn in 1924. It was found directly on top of the egg nest AMNH 6508.

specimens.name: Associated nest
specimens.note: The clutch of elongated eggs beneath the holotype, originally assigned to Protoceratops; later embryo finds showed such eggs are oviraptorid.

panel.headline: One crushed skeleton on a nest, and a name that outgrew it.
panel.standfirst: Oviraptor philoceratops rests on a single incomplete skeleton with a badly crushed skull, found lying over a clutch of eggs at the Flaming Cliffs in 1923. Most of the complete oviraptorid skeletons displayed as Oviraptor belong to Citipati.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: The holotype preserves the skull, parts of the vertebral column, the shoulder girdle and forelimbs, the pelvis and some hindlimb bones, but the skull is shattered, the tail is largely missing and no second individual is securely referred.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: A crushed and disarticulated skull with lower jaws, cervical and dorsal vertebrae, ribs, a furcula and shoulder girdle, both forelimbs with hands, the pelvis and partial hindlimbs, all from one animal, plus the nest of eggs it lay upon.
knownRemains.note: Because only one specimen is securely assigned, growth, variation and the true crest profile cannot be assessed. Anatomy described from referred Zamyn Khondt material is now attributed to Citipati.

media.title: Holotype skull AMNH 6517 as figured by Osborn in 1924
media.alt: Published 1924 drawing of the crushed Oviraptor philoceratops holotype skull, AMNH 6517, in right and left views
media.caption: Osborn's figure of the type skull exactly as it lay in the sandstone, with the shattered bones drawn in outline. The crushing is why the crest shape remains debated.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A complete but shattered skull and lower jaws, toothless, with the base of a crest preserved in poor condition.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical and dorsal vertebrae with ribs; the sacrum is partly known and the tail is largely missing.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Furcula, scapulocoracoids, both forelimbs with three-fingered hands, the pelvis and partial hindlimb bones.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Direct association with a nest of oviraptorid eggs; reported lizard bones in the body cavity. No feathers, skin or colour are preserved.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 6517 · holotype
specimenCards.description: Collected by George Olsen in 1923 during the third Central Asiatic Expedition and described by Osborn in 1924. The skull was found crushed flat in the sandstone directly above the eggs, which led to the original egg-thief interpretation.
specimenCards.meta: Bayn Dzak, Mongolia · Djadokhta Formation · American Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: AMNH 6508 · egg clutch
specimenCards.description: The elongated eggs beneath the skeleton were assigned to Protoceratops in 1924. Embryos found in matching eggs in 1993 showed they belong to oviraptorids, reinterpreting the holotype as a probable brooding adult.
specimenCards.meta: Same site as the holotype · eggs of the elongatoolithid type

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: One incomplete skeleton with a crushed toothless skull, long clawed hands and a pelvis, lying on a clutch of oviraptorid-type eggs.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A feathered, bipedal oviraptorid that was probably brooding its own nest; feathering and brooding posture are inferred from close relatives such as Citipati.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The shape of the crest, the complete skull outline, adult size range, tail anatomy, diet, and which if any other specimens belong to the genus.
